[1;97m1.4 — the shell, caught in the act[0m

Type [92mdate[0m. Now type [92mdtae[0m.

  [92mdate[0m     [90m# prints the date and time[0m
  [92mdtae[0m     [90m# bash: dtae: command not found[0m

Read who is speaking. [92mbash:[0m is the shell. It looked for a
program called dtae, found none, and told you. When the name is
right, it finds the program and runs it; what the program prints
comes back to you.

Three parts, kept apart for the rest of this tutor:
  [36mterminal[0m  →  [36mshell[0m  →  [36mprogram[0m
The terminal is the window. The shell is the program named [92mbash[0m
that read your line. [92mdate[0m is the program it ran.

[1;97m1.5 — who else types here[0m

Everything you typed went terminal → shell → program. There is no
other way in: anything that runs a command on this machine goes
through a shell the same way.

An AI assistant that "runs commands" for you is no exception. It
types a line into a shell; the shell finds the program; the program
runs. The line it typed can be read exactly as you read your own.

So the habits in this course count twice:
  [36mread the line[0m before anyone presses Enter — you, or a helper
  [36mknow the folder[0m it will run in
  [36mread the output[0m when it comes back, instead of skimming it

[91mThe most important idea in this stage.[0m When you open a file in
Vim, Vim [36mreads it into a buffer[0m — a copy in memory. Your
keystrokes change the [36mbuffer[0m, not the file. The file on disk
only changes when you [36mwrite[0m the buffer back.

  [36mfile on disk[0m  →  [36mbuffer in memory[0m  →  [36mfile on disk[0m
       (read)                  (edit)                     (write)

That's why Vim has separate commands for save and quit:
  [92m:w[0m    write the buffer to the file
  [92m:q[0m    quit (only if there are no unsaved changes)
  [92m:q![0m   quit and discard unsaved changes
  [92m:wq[0m   write, then quit
